set.approach: Amphitheater Road leaves US 550 above town, and the drainage below its end holds the Portland Creek gully system. From the end of the road, drop into the drainage and follow the prominent gully on the right (east), passing a difficult chockstone on its left. The line follows the striking couloir up the middle of the bowl, and several cruxes begin with getting into the main couloir itself. Avalanche hazard here can be severe. Check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: The line climbs to the main ridge above treeline. Getting down is awkward because the terrain around the route is loose, broken rock, so plan the descent before leaving the ridge. Easy alpine ice and snow separate the waterfall pitches, which matters if you need to downclimb or rappel. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page gives the line, avalanche warning and the loose-terrain descent remark; Portland Creek page gives the drainage and the gully on the right. One source each; no counts.

set.approach: Climb the Amphitheater Route gully (the south branch of Portland Creek) to the prominent smears on the left, north-facing wall, set just below the big blue slab pitch and well up the gully. They cannot be seen from town below, but are hard to miss once you are close and the ice has formed. Check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: If the short upper curtain has formed, traverse right along the rim and rappel into the gully at any point where the cliff is short enough for your ropes to reach. If it has not formed, V-thread off the last steep ice on the route itself rather than continuing higher. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: PDX page gives location off the Amphitheater gully and both descent options. No counts used.

set.approach: Park before the bridge over Portland Creek on Amphitheater Road. Take the trail on the right side of the bridge; the short flow sits just beyond. It is set up as a top-rope, with two bolts at the top.

review.notes: Route page: trail right of bridge, top bolts. Area page: parking before the bridge on Amphitheater Rd. Descent not stated; not written.

set.approach: From the end of the road, drop into the Portland Creek drainage and head up the prominent gully on the right (east), going left around a difficult chockstone. For Portland Creek proper, leave that gully by breaking left up a narrow slot choked with chockstones after a short distance. Much of the ice can be seen from town, and a large amount of vertical gain lies between the road and the first real ice. Check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel the upper flows from V-threads or trees; the last flow is best threaded. From the top, walk off west and either find a hidden chute into the larger northwest-facing gully (only with high snow) or rappel into the same gully. Rappelling all the way down the route is also possible but slow. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Single detailed route page for approach and descent; no counts used.

set.approach: From Highway 82 east of Aspen take Lincoln Creek Road past Grizzly Reservoir to the Anderson and Petroleum trailhead on the right. Snow may stop vehicles short of the trailhead in the colder months, lengthening the walk. Hike the trail west to Anderson Lake, directly under the north face. The couloir is the one that tops out just right (west) of the apparent high point; its serpentine shape makes conditions hard to judge from the lake.
set.descent_text: Descend the west ridge to gentler north-facing couloirs and slopes. You can also continue along the ridge to Petroleum Peak and go down its east ridge or face. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page for line and descent; area page for road, trailhead and lake. Mileage left out (single source).

set.approach: Begin at the Glacier Gorge trailhead and walk toward Andrews Glacier. At Andrews Tarn, near the foot of the glacier, climb up the glacier while trending to the left. The couloir hugs the rock wall on that side, and you are at its start when a snow, ice and rock ramp heads south. Small crevasses near the bottom of the glacier can be deep, so take care around them.
set.descent_text: After the ice, the route turns to fourth and low fifth class rock; move right near the top to finish in an alpine meadow. Hike over to Andrews Glacier, descend it, and rejoin the main trail back to the trailhead.

review.notes: Route page gives approach, crevasse note and the glacier descent. No counts.

set.approach: From the Glacier Gorge trailhead, follow the trail to The Loch and continue a little farther to the log bridge over Andrews Creek, where a sign points to Andrews Glacier. In the snowy months this trail is lightly used and can be hard to follow; if in doubt, stay with the creek. It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west. The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth. Brain Freeze begins low on the left of the Solar Wall, a south-facing section of Otis, in a big left-facing corner, and follows the same early ground as the standard line there.
set.descent_text: If visibility is poor and you do not know the descent, rappel the route. Otherwise descend along the east ridge until you see a wide clearing on your right, then head south through the trees, bearing right to meet the Andrews Creek trail. The snow gully just west of the route is another way down and leads straight to the base.

review.notes: Route page gives the start and both descents; area page gives the approach trail.

set.approach: From the Glacier Gorge trailhead, follow the trail to The Loch and continue a little farther to the log bridge over Andrews Creek, where a sign points to Andrews Glacier. In the snowy months this trail is lightly used and can be hard to follow; if in doubt, stay with the creek. It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west. The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth. The line sits between Zowie and Wham on Otis Peak's south side, and starts with steps kicked up gully snow into a sheltered cave under the first chockstone.
set.descent_text: Walk off to the right, the same way as Wham Couloir, or rappel the route. In a whiteout the walk-off is hard to locate, and straying may force a rappel.

review.notes: Route page gives location and descent; area page the approach.

It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west. The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth. The climb is a southwest-facing outcrop on the way to the back side of Sharkstooth. Pass the buttress as you start up the talus and look back to see it.

review.notes: Route page gives location; area page the approach. Descent not stated.

set.approach: From the Glacier Gorge trailhead, follow the trail to The Loch and continue a little farther to the log bridge over Andrews Creek, where a sign points to Andrews Glacier. In the snowy months this trail is lightly used and can be hard to follow; if in doubt, stay with the creek. It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west. The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth. Flour Power starts in The Gash below the headwall under Andrews Tarn and climbs the south face of Otis Peak, finishing just east of the summit. It faces south and a big snowfield sits above it, so it is prone to slides early in the season. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page gives start, aspect and exit; area page the approach. Descent not stated.

set.approach: From the Glacier Gorge trailhead, follow the trail to The Loch and continue a little farther to the log bridge over Andrews Creek, where a sign points to Andrews Glacier. In the snowy months this trail is lightly used and can be hard to follow; if in doubt, stay with the creek. It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west. The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth. Approach as for Sharkstooth. Below the north base of Sharkstooth, look to your right (west) and Forbidden Tower stands out on the right side of the Gash wall. Start at the lowest right-hand rock band, below the chimney system, and aim for the left side of the large cave at its base.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route. The summit of Forbidden Tower has a sling for the first rappel, and a fixed station lower down is used on the way. The last rappel puts you on the snowfield, which can be glissaded back to your stash, but once the snow melts back that last rappel may no longer reach.

review.notes: Route page gives start and rappel descent; area page the approach. Rappel counts left out.

It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west. The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth. The route begins partway up Brain Freeze, at the base of the obvious ice column on the left wall of the gully. Getting there is easy climbing or hiking.
set.descent_text: Traverse right at the top and rappel Brain Freeze. The alternative is one of several easy lines through the short cliff band above, then descending the gully on the west side to reach the foot of Brain Freeze.

review.notes: Production page gives start and both descents; Brain Freeze page and area page the approach.

In the snowy months this trail is lightly used and can be hard to follow; if in doubt, stay with the creek. It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west. The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth. Wham Couloir is a tight gully directly right of the Wham spire, on Otis Peak's south side. Seen from the trail only the direct start is visible; a second, ice start is hidden on the left.
set.descent_text: Walk east until you can see trees toward the top of a south-facing slope that leads back toward the Andrews Creek drainage. Follow the trees down to stay out of avalanche terrain, then bend right to return to the base of the route. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: Route page gives start and the walk-off; area page the approach.

set.approach: Camp Bird Road (CR 361) passes Angel Creek Campground; use the big pullout there, on the right when driving up from town. Head north-northwest on the campground road and trails toward Angel Creek. From there there are two ways to the ice: a high traverse above the drainage, or following the creek itself. The creek way becomes steep-walled, with big boulders, chockstones and rubble to get past; if frozen they are easy ice steps, but they may be wet and hard mixed with a pool below. The high traverse is probably safer. In an average winter bring snowshoes. Check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route from trees, willows and V-threads, walking between the steps. In the drainage, downclimb the easy sections or traverse to the cluster of leaning trees west of the creek to rappel the lowest step, then walk out the way you came.

review.notes: Route page for approach choices and descent; area page for parking. Rappel and rope counts left out.

set.approach: Camp Bird Road (CR 361) passes Angel Creek Campground; use the big pullout there, on the right when driving up from town. The flow is easy to spot from the road. Walk west into the trees, through light brush, until you reach an opening where the route comes into view. Check the avalanche forecast.
set.descent_text: Rappel the route from the anchors, with the descent broken at the stance below the steeper ice.

review.notes: Route page for approach and descent; area page for parking. No time counts.

set.approach: From the lower (western) ski parking lot at Arapahoe Basin, hike west along US 6 downhill, then pick a way down to the river. It is better to go a little too far downstream, since cliffs wall off the canyon; then work back up along the river to the falls. Snowshoes are advisable.

review.notes: Route page for approach; area page for US 6 and parking. Distance left out (single source).

set.approach: Approach from the Glacier Gorge trailhead past Mills Lake and on to Black Lake or Solitude Lake. Deep snow is likely for most of the winter. Deborah is the conspicuous couloir that cuts the peak's south side. Two ways reach it: the west gully rising out of Black Lake, or a longer walk round to the south side, then straight to the foot of the couloir.

review.notes: Route page gives the couloir and two ways to its base; area page the trailhead and lakes. Descent only referenced to another page; not written.

set.approach: Approach from the Glacier Gorge trailhead past Mills Lake and on to Black Lake or Solitude Lake. Deep snow is likely for most of the winter. The line is on the north face of Arrowhead, to the right of The Hourglass Couloir, above Solitude Lake.

review.notes: Route page: location right of the Hourglass; Hourglass page: north face above Solitude Lake. Descent not stated.

set.approach: Approach from the Glacier Gorge trailhead past Mills Lake and on to Black Lake or Solitude Lake. Deep snow is likely for most of the winter. The Hourglass is the gully at the centre of Arrowhead's north side, straight above Solitude Lake.
set.descent_text: Descend the southeast gully to Black Lake, which may require some rappels.

review.notes: Route page gives location and southeast gully descent; area page the approach.

set.approach: Start from the Guanella Pass road, where the winter closure sits on its north side, and hike to the top of the pass. Follow the Mount Bierstadt trail until it is clear you should bear left (northeast) into the Scott Gomer Creek drainage. Continue up the creek into the basin below the Sawtooth, to just below the highest alpine lakes. Winter closure of the road makes the approach long. The flow is a short, secluded one.

review.notes: Route and area pages agree on the pass, trail and creek; mileage left out (single source). Descent not stated.

set.approach: The flow is the large slab of ice low on the west face of the mountain, across the gully east of the Huerfano road. Leave the road when you are level with the ice, hike down to the river, cross it and climb back up to the base. Reaching it is the hard part, with a long snowshoe walk along the road and a creek crossing. FUNdus takes the steepest line, straight up the centre of the flow, right of The Birth Canal.
set.descent_text: Bushwhack through the willows at the top to a conifer with slings and a rappel ring, and rappel from there.

review.notes: Route page for line, approach hardships and the rappel tree; area page for the approach. No counts.

set.approach: The flow is the large slab of ice low on the west face of the mountain, across the gully east of the Huerfano road. Leave the road when you are level with the ice, hike down to the river, cross it and climb back up to the base. Reaching it is the hard part, with a long snowshoe walk along the road and a creek crossing. The Birth Canal begins on the far left of the big flow: climb through a hole in the ice to emerge onto the main sheet.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the slung tree near the upper left end of the flow; the rope has to be long enough to reach the base.

review.notes: Route page for start and rappel tree; area page for approach.

set.approach: Hike the Lily Lake trail along Huerfano Creek as far as its final switchback. Cross snowfields and go up a narrow, steep snow runnel to reach the basin below the north face. The Gash Couloir is the obvious couloir on the left side of the face, leading up to the Gash on Gash Ridge. Rockfall and ice fall are heavy when the right wall catches early sun.
set.descent_text: The couloir tops out on Gash Ridge, which can be followed to the summit. Options from there include downclimbing the angling snow couloir to the right of Ormes Buttress, or going over Ellingwood Point and down ledges; the route itself can be rappelled but the rock is rotten and rockfall is frequent. A steep, snowy ridge can be downclimbed to a snowfield and then the basin below the face.

review.notes: Single detailed route page; no counts used.

set.approach: Follow the Lily Lake trail to the first switchback, then cross snow to the base. The route is a narrow couloir on the north wall between Blanca and Ellingwood, which runs up to the col between the two peaks. The climb uses the lower section, then veers left into a somewhat broader gully that stays in shade.
set.descent_text: One way down is to rappel off the ridge back onto the snow ramp, downclimb the ramp to the fixed pin and rappel from it onto steep alpine ice, which can be downclimbed or rappelled to the ramp. Next, move right along the ramp to a point beneath Ellingwood and glissade down into the bowl under the face.

review.notes: Single detailed route page; rope lengths left out.

set.approach: Start from the Long Lake trailhead off Brainard Lake Road and follow the valley trail to Lake Isabelle; the road is gated in winter and spring, which adds distance. The flow is easy to pick out from the lake, up on the valley's north wall at the western end. The left side of the flow is lower angle, with the right side steeper rock and ice.
set.descent_text: The easiest descent is to walk off the top and join the Pawnee Pass trail.

review.notes: Route page for location and descent; area page for roads and trailheads. Mileage left out.

set.approach: From the Mitchell Lake trailhead off Brainard Lake Road, walk west beyond Mitchell Lake and Blue Lake, aiming for the gap in the skyline north of Mount Toll. Short of that gap, an evident couloir appears on the east side of the north ridge. In winter the road is gated, which adds a long approach.
set.descent_text: The couloir leads to the summit. The easiest way down is the south face, which has slid on warm spring days, so time your climb accordingly.

review.notes: Route page for line and descent; area page for trailhead and road gate.

set.approach: Leave the car at the seasonal gate where County Road 30 ends, then walk the Cataract Gulch trail up through the forest. Once out of the trees, climbs on both the east and west sides of the gulch are reachable. Check the avalanche forecast. Chockstone Gully lies on the creek's east bank directly opposite Fight Club, in a chimney at the foot of a wide drainage.

review.notes: Route page for location; area page for road and trail. Descent not stated.

set.approach: Leave the car at the seasonal gate where County Road 30 ends, then walk the Cataract Gulch trail up through the forest. Once out of the trees, climbs on both the east and west sides of the gulch are reachable. Check the avalanche forecast. Fight Club sits about halfway up the gulch, beyond Unknown WI4 (Second Couloir), right of the trail, on the north-facing side of a couloir.
set.descent_text: Use a tree to the right at the top for a rappel, or walk off by heading down and left.

review.notes: Route page for location and descent; area page for road and trail.

set.approach: Leave the car at the seasonal gate where County Road 30 ends, then walk the Cataract Gulch trail up through the forest. Once out of the trees, climbs on both the east and west sides of the gulch are reachable. Check the avalanche forecast. No Fight Left lies across on the creek's west bank, in the broad drainage to the left of Fight Club. Another way in is to finish Fight Club and cross left over the wide bench.

review.notes: Route page for location; area page for road and trail. Descent not stated.

set.approach: Leave the car at the seasonal gate where County Road 30 ends, then walk the Cataract Gulch trail up through the forest. Once out of the trees, climbs on both the east and west sides of the gulch are reachable. Check the avalanche forecast. This is one of the first lines on your left as you leave the trees; plough through the snow to its base.
set.descent_text: The top ends at a tree anchor up and right, from which parties rappel.

review.notes: Route page for location and anchor; area page for road and trail.

set.approach: Follow the forest road from Highway 17 to the trailhead, which sits down a short side road on the left. Ford the Chama River and use trails to reach the ice in the upper west fork; a motorized sled may be needed in winter to cover the road. Banded Falls fills the left-hand one of three gullies that face north beside West Fork Chama Falls.

review.notes: Route and area pages; descent not stated.

set.approach: Follow the forest road from Highway 17 to the trailhead, which sits down a short side road on the left. Mr. Bones' Wild Ride fills the centre gully of that trio, flanked by Banded Falls and The Ghost.

review.notes: Route and area pages; descent not stated.

set.approach: Follow the forest road from Highway 17 to the trailhead, which sits down a short side road on the left. The Ghost is the right-hand gully of the three and holds the most sustained steep ice among those north-facing lines.

review.notes: Route and area pages; descent not stated.

set.approach: Follow the forest road from Highway 17 to the trailhead, which sits down a short side road on the left. Ford the Chama River and use trails to reach the ice in the upper west fork; a motorized sled may be needed in winter to cover the road. The Twoloir is a wide couloir further left, past Banded Falls.

review.notes: Route and area pages; descent not stated.

set.approach: Park at Bear Lake in Rocky Mountain National Park and hike the packed trail to Nymph Lake; snowshoes are recommended. The ice is hidden in the trees and only the top of some of it can be seen from the lake, near the restoration-area sign. Take a bearing from there and head through the trees, staying low in the basin, because there is a steep slope with avalanche potential just right of the ice if you contour. As you near the cliffs you will see bits of ice well above you; head up. You can also drop into the drainage below the ice from the trail between Nymph and Dream Lakes, but that is harder. The area faces south. Check the avalanche forecast. Olympic Trials is the small prow of ice in the middle of the lower cliff band, just below the upper tier.

review.notes: Route and area pages; descent not stated.

set.approach: Park at Bear Lake and take the winter trail toward Nymph Lake and Chaos. The cliff is south-facing, on otherwise north-south cliffs, a little above and south of the winter track linking Nymph Lake and Chaos. Follow the skin track that heads over toward lower Chaos and up; the cliff is on your right, and the route is around the first corner you reach.

review.notes: Route page for location; area page for Bear Lake start. Descent not stated.

set.descent_text: Rappel off trees or walk off to the left.

review.notes: Route and area pages.

Reach it by climbing the candle-like ice beneath it onto a shelf.
set.descent_text: Anchor from a large tree at the top and rappel, or walk off to the left.

review.notes: Route and area pages.

co_cascade_mountain_ice_gnar_couloir.skip_reason: No readable page for this ice line; the only Gnar Couloir found is a snow climb on a different peak, so it does not fit the stored grade.
